items.title: UK GDPR, Article 15: Right of access by the data subject
items.locator: Art. 15(1)(h), 15(1A) and 15(3); textual amendment notes F4, F5 and F8
items.quote: based on a reasonable and proportionate search for the personal data and other information described in that paragraph
items.why: The access right. Paragraph 1A limits it to what a reasonable and proportionate search can provide; inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.78(1)(a), in force at Royal Assent (s.142(2)(b)) and treated as in force from 1 January 2024 (s.78(5)). Point (h) requires meaningful information about the logic of automated decisions that are subject to the Article 22C safeguards. Year is the year of the latest amendment shown.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 17: Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten')
items.quote: the controller shall have the obligation to erase personal data without undue delay where one of the following grounds applies
items.why: The erasure duty and its limits: it applies only on the listed grounds (for example data no longer necessary, consent withdrawn, a successful objection, unlawful processing) and not where paragraph 3 applies. Nothing in the article excludes data held in AI systems. Read with Article 19 (telling recipients) and Article 11 (where the person cannot be identified).

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 21: Right to object
items.quote: The controller shall no longer process the personal data unless the controller demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds for the processing
items.why: The objection right, expressly including profiling. It applies only where the lawful basis is Article 6(1)(e), (ea) or (f), and the controller may continue on compelling legitimate grounds; the objection to direct marketing in paragraphs 2 and 3 has no such exception. '(ea)' added 5 February 2026 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.70(5).

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How do we ensure individual rights in our AI systems?
items.locator: Sections 'How should we ensure individual rights requests for training data?', 'How should we ensure individual rights requests for AI outputs?' and 'How do individual rights relate to data contained in the model itself?'
items.quote: When procuring an AI service, you must choose one which allows individual rights to be protected and enabled
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation (training data section). Rights apply to training data, to inputs and outputs in deployment, and to data contained in a model. Requests are not manifestly unfounded or excessive just because AI makes them harder; erasing training data does not mean erasing the model unless the model contains the data or can be used to infer it; rectification or erasure inside a model may need re-training or deletion. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Year not shown on the page; follows earlier reading lists, to confirm.

items.title: Response to the consultation series on generative AI: Engineering individual rights into generative AI models
items.locator: Section 'Our response'; also 'In brief' and 'Key points from the responses'
items.quote: these may not be sufficient, as they do not actually remove the data from the model
items.why: The regulator's stated position, not statutory guidance: organisations must have mechanisms to fulfil requests for training data and, if a model contains personal data, for the model itself; output filters may not be enough; Article 11 must not be used to avoid obligations; no clear evidence was received of practical measures, and machine unlearning was argued mainly in theory. The page shows no publication date, so the year is the year it was read; it refers to the Data (Use and Access) Bill, so it predates the 2025 Act.

items.title: Right of access: How do we find and retrieve the relevant information?
items.locator: Sections 'What efforts do we need to make to find information?', 'What about archived information and backup records?' and 'What about personal information in big datasets?'
items.quote: However, there is no technology exemption from the right of access.
items.why: How far a search must go after the 2025 Act: reasonable and proportionate, and the organisation must be able to show why a search would not be. Observed and inferred information about a person is within the right. Expects adequate metadata and the ability to query for everything held about one person. Date is the 'latest updates' date shown on the page. The companion page on preparing for requests recommends information asset registers and a request log.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, artificial intelligence toolkit: Contracts and third parties
items.locator: List beginning 'Include terms or clauses stating that'
items.quote: the processor must take appropriate measures to help the controller respond to requests from people to exercise their rights
items.why: What the regulator's auditors look for in AI supplier contracts; the underlying duty is UK GDPR Article 28(3)(e). The toolkit has no separate section on individual rights. 'Under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year it was read.

items.title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
items.locator: Para. 43 (p. 16); also para. 65 (p. 21) and the lists of mitigating measures on pp. 29-30 and para. 114 (p. 32)
items.quote: By default, SAs should consider that AI models are likely to require a thorough evaluation of the likelihood of identification
items.why: EU comparator on whether a trained model still holds personal data, which decides whether rights reach the model. A model is anonymous only if the likelihood of extracting personal data, directly or through queries, is insignificant. Lists unlearning and erasure beyond the legal minimum as mitigating measures, and notes that regulators may order erasure of a dataset or a model. Not binding in the UK.

items.title: 2025 Coordinated Enforcement Action: Implementation of the right to erasure by controllers
items.quote: a total of 764 controllers responded to the questionnaire
items.why: Source of the figure. Seven recurring issues, the first being 'Absence of a documented and updated internal procedure to handle erasure requests'; others include erasure in back-ups and weak anonymisation used in place of deletion. Covers erasure generally, not AI, and the European Economic Area, not the UK. The PDF gives the adoption date as 10 February 2026.

items.title: Machine Unlearning Doesn't Do What You Think: Lessons for Generative AI Policy and Research
items.quote: unlearning is not a general-purpose solution for circumscribing generative-AI model behavior in service of broader positive impact
items.why: Research support for caution about promising to remove one person's data from a trained model: the authors identify mismatches between what unlearning aims at and what can be implemented. Abstract only read in this pass; version 2 dated 31 October 2025.
